name: Coffee / green tea ritual
lead: The coffee or green tea ritual refers to drinking caffeinated beverages as part of a routine aimed at reducing facial puffiness or improving appearance. Both beverages contain caffeine, and green tea also contains polyphenols such as EGCG [1][2].

Caffeine can briefly increase urine output after large single doses in people not accustomed to it, but regular users develop tolerance [2]. Wikipedia reports that green tea polyphenols have no proven biological effects in humans and that health claims were not supported by sufficient evidence in a 2011 EFSA review [1]. No studies found on drinking either beverage to reduce facial puffiness.
infobox: Up to 400 mg/day for non-pregnant adults [2]

paras: Practitioners drink coffee or green tea, often in the morning, in the belief that caffeine or tea antioxidants reduce water retention or improve skin. Green tea originated in China and spread across East Asia [1].

No studies found on drinking coffee or green tea for facial puffiness. General green tea research reports small blood pressure reductions and lower cholesterol in a 2013 Cochrane analysis, but no good evidence for weight loss, and no significant effect on C-reactive protein in a 2015 meta-analysis [1].

EFSA considers up to 400 mg of caffeine per day not a safety concern for non-pregnant adults, and 200 mg for pregnant or lactating women. Caffeine can delay sleep, and doses as low as 100 mg per day may disrupt sleep in some people [2]. High-dose green tea extracts have been linked to liver toxicity, and Health Canada recommended a warning label in 2017; traditionally brewed tea is considered safe by EFSA with rare liver damage [1].

card.summary: Caffeine drinks used as a de-puffing routine; no study has tested the face effect.
card.note: Caffeine affects sleep; high-dose tea extracts linked to liver injury.

quick.overview:
People drink coffee or green tea as a daily ritual intended to reduce puffiness.

Caffeine has a short-lived diuretic effect in non-habitual users, but no published trial has tested these drinks for facial appearance.
quick.mechanism: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors and may increase urine output briefly; tolerance develops with regular use [2].
quick.risks: Caffeine can disrupt sleep. Concentrated green tea extracts have been associated with liver toxicity [1][2].
